label: Build stage
why: Tells us when your heating system will be needed, so your design is ready in time.
step_intro: Check what we have from your quote, and tell us who to talk to about the design.

label: Has the date you need the goods changed?
hint: We show the date we hold beside this. Only fill it in if it's different.

label: Who should we talk to about the design, if not you?
why: If a builder or architect is handling the detail, we'll go to them first and keep you copied.
placeholder: Name, role and mobile, e.g. Dave, site manager, 07…

label: what3words for the site (optional)
placeholder: ///word.word.word

label: Are the plans we hold still the current ones?
hint: Yes means nothing has changed since the quote. No means there's a newer revision: add it below.
why: Plans change between quote and build. We design from the newest revision we hold, so a wall moved or a kitchen island added after the quote won't be on our drawings unless you send the new version. Not sure which revision we have? Say so in Anything else and we'll check with you.
step_intro: We designed your quote from the plans you sent us. We just need to know they're still current, and anything the plans don't show.

label: New or extra files (optional)
hint: PDF, DWG, photos or ZIP, up to 10 MB each.

label: I have files bigger than 10 MB
hint: Don't worry: tick this and your Project Engineer will send you a secure file request so you can send them directly.

label: Ceiling heights
hint: If your plans include sections, just say so. Otherwise assume 2.4 m and list any rooms that differ.
why: A good set of plans includes sections showing ceiling heights. Without them we need the height of every room and any vaulted areas, because the room volume sets its heat requirement.
placeholder: e.g. sections on the plans. Or: 2.4 m everywhere except the kitchen-diner, vaulted to 4.2 m

label: Windows and external doors
hint: If your plans include elevations, just say so. Otherwise standard windows are about 1.2 m tall; tell us about bifolds, picture windows or lots of glazing.
why: Elevations show windows and doors to scale. With only floor plans we have the widths but not the heights, and glazing is where most heat is lost.
placeholder: e.g. elevations on the plans. Or: living room has 4 m bifold doors

label: Anywhere we shouldn't heat?
why: We keep pipe out from under fitted units, islands, baths, showers and staircases. A kitchen or bathroom drawing, even a sketch, stops us heating under your island.
placeholder: e.g. under the kitchen island and the bath. Garage and plant room unheated. Open staircase.

label: Pick whichever is easiest
options: Upload the SAP calculation|Use my EPC|Describe it|New build: use the standard minimums
why: Your design service includes a heat loss calculation for every room, which sizes the heat pump and the pipe. For that we need to know how well the walls, windows, roof and floor keep heat in. A SAP calculation or an EPC already says; otherwise a rough description is enough, and for a new build we can use the Building Regulations minimums.
step_intro: This sizes your system. Pick whichever of the four is easiest; a rough description is fine.

label: SAP calculation or EPC
hint: The full SAP calculation if you have it, not just the summary page.

label: Age of the property, or year built
hint: A mix of ages (an extension on an old house)? Say which rooms are which.
placeholder: e.g. new build 2026, or 1930s with a 2015 extension

label: Walls
placeholder: Construction and insulation thickness

label: Windows
placeholder: Double or triple glazed, frame type

label: Roof
placeholder: Insulation thickness

label: Floors
placeholder: Concrete, timber or beam and block; insulation thickness

label: Walls
why: For an existing house we work out how much heat each part loses from what it's made of and how old it is.
placeholder: Age, thickness, brick/stone/timber/cob, cavity filled?

label: Windows
placeholder: Age, single/double/triple glazed, wood/metal/uPVC

label: Roof
placeholder: Age and insulation thickness

label: Floors
placeholder: Age, concrete/timber/beam and block, insulation if any

label: Where would you like the manifold(s)?
why: Each manifold feeds the pipe loops around it, so its position sets how the loops are laid out and how far the pipe runs. A cupboard near the middle of the floor it serves is ideal. Mark them on the plans if it's easier to show than to say.
step_intro: Where the manifolds go, and a few details about your floors.
placeholder: e.g. utility room cupboard, and the airing cupboard upstairs. Or: marked on the plans

label: Your boiler: type and where it is
why: The boiler type decides how we connect the underfloor heating and whether a cylinder is involved.
placeholder: Combi, system or regular boiler, and the room it's in

label: Your heat pump: make, model and where it will go
why: We design the underfloor heating to suit the heat pump's flow temperature, so we need to know which one it is.

label: Your heat source and where it is
Hot water cylinder, if there is one
placeholder: e.g. airing cupboard upstairs. Or: none, combi boiler

label: Screed floors: liquid or hand-mixed, and the depth
why: Liquid screed flows round the pipe and can be thinner; hand-mixed needs more depth over the pipe. The depth sets how quickly the floor warms up.
placeholder: e.g. liquid screed, 50 mm over the pipe

label: Joisted floors: joist type, direction and spacing, and any steels
hint: Joist type: Posi, TJI/I-joist, Eco or traditional timber. If the joist layout is on your plans, just say so. Steels: where they are and whether there's a 25 mm gap above or below them.
why: We draw the pipe between the joists, so we need their direction and spacing in each room. Engineered joists (Eco, TJI, Posi) let the pipe cross anywhere. Traditional timber joists have to be notched or battened, which limits where it can cross. Steels need a 25 mm gap for the pipe to pass, or they must be drilled, which your structural engineer has to agree.
placeholder: e.g. I-joists front to back at 400 mm centres; one steel over the kitchen with a gap above

label: Joist drawing or a photo of the floor from below (optional)
Floor coverings, room by room
why: Carpet and thick wood slow the heat getting through, so the pipe spacing and flow temperature change with the covering.
placeholder: e.g. tiles in kitchen and bathrooms, engineered wood in living room, carpet in bedrooms

label: Can pipes run through internal walls if needed?
why: Sometimes the shortest route to a room is through a wall rather than round it.

label: Where will the heat pump go?
why: An air source heat pump must be more than 1 m from the boundary to count as permitted development (3 m in Wales). Closer than that needs a planning application. It also needs clear airflow around it.
step_intro: Where it will go, what's around it, and how close the neighbours are. We use this to check the heat pump will be quiet enough for them, which is part of signing the installation off. A quick walk outside with your phone answers most of it.
placeholder: e.g. north gable wall by the utility room, 2.5 m from the fence. Or: marked on my plans

label: A photo of the spot (optional)
hint: It answers most of the questions below for us.

label: What will be close to it?
options: On a wall, open around it|In a corner, or a fence within a metre|Boxed in on more than two sides
why: Walls and fences within about a metre bounce the sound back, so the more there are, the louder it seems next door. The ground always counts as one. Up to three is fine; boxed in on all sides usually isn't, so we'd suggest another spot.

label: How far is the heat pump from your nearest neighbour's window or door?
hint: In metres, roughly. Pacing it out is fine: one big step is about a metre. Count windows and doors of rooms they live in, not a garage or hallway.
why: The rule is about how loud the heat pump is just outside your neighbours' windows and doors. Think about every neighbour who could see the spot, not only the closest; if more than one is near, tell us about each at the end of this step.
placeholder: e.g. 8

label: Which window or door is it?
placeholder: e.g. the kitchen window of number 6, across the side passage

label: What's between the heat pump and that window?
options: Nothing, or a hedge or open fence|A thin wooden fence (solid, no gaps)|A brick wall or thick solid fence
why: A solid wall or thick fence between the two takes a good deal of the sound away. Hedges and fences with gaps don't count, however tall.

label: Standing at that window, how much of the heat pump would you see?
options: All of it|Part of it|None of it, it's hidden
why: If the heat pump is hidden from the window, the sound reaching it is lower.

label: Any other neighbours close by? (optional)
placeholder: e.g. number 10 behind us: bedroom window about 12 m away over a 1.8 m brick wall

label: Cylinder, buffer tank and expansion vessels: where will they go?
why: We check your quoted cylinder and buffer actually fit the space (a cylinder up to 300 l can sit on a square 100 l buffer). There can be up to three expansion vessels.
placeholder: e.g. plant room off the utility, 1.2 m × 2 m, 2.4 m high

label: Bedrooms
hint: We size hot water for bedrooms + 1 people unless you tell us otherwise.
placeholder: e.g. 4

label: Ground source only: ground collector area or borehole
hint: Your quote states the area and pipe length allowed for; tell us where it will go, or mark up a site plan.

label: Anything else
step_intro: Anything unusual, or something you'd like changed.
